hook: One in four Texas listings did something quiet last month.

scores.worst_problem: The hook's withheld element is the most guessable thing in real estate right now — 'did something quiet' resolves to 'cut the price' for most readers before they swipe, and slide 1 confirms exactly that.
scores.fix: Rewrite the hook so the withheld piece is the consequence rather than the action — e.g. 'One in four Texas listings quietly did the one thing sellers swore they wouldn't' — and make slide 1's payoff the number, not the reveal.

deck.hook: One in four Texas listings did something quiet last month.

points.title: The Quiet Price Cut
body: Roughly one in four active Texas listings took a price reduction last month.
That is not a crash. That is sellers meeting the number buyers will actually pay.
points.loop: The cause is hiding in plain sight.

points.title: Buyers Have Options Again
body: There are more homes sitting on the Texas market than we have seen in over a decade.
A buyer can tour eight houses in a weekend and walk away from all eight.
points.loop: Choice does something strange to people.

points.title: Priced For A Market That Ended
body: Plenty of sellers are still anchored to what their neighbor got three years ago.
The buyer is not comparing your house to 2022. They are comparing it to the eleven others open right now.
points.loop: There is a clock on that mistake.

points.title: The First Three Weeks
body: Homes that sell almost always find their buyer early.
Miss that window and showings thin out, and every offer after that comes in lower than the one you turned down.
points.loop: Price is only half of the problem.

points.title: Everything Is Negotiable Now
body: Buyers are asking for rate buydowns, closing costs, and repairs. Often all three.
A seller paying those is not desperate anymore. That is just what a deal looks like this year.
points.loop: Your zip code is not the average.

linkedinCaption:
Roughly one in four active Texas listings took a price reduction last month. That is not a crash. That is sellers adjusting to the number buyers will actually pay.

Inventory is the highest it has been in over a decade. A buyer can tour eight homes in a weekend and pass on all eight. That changes how pricing works.

The first three weeks still decide most outcomes. Homes that sell find their buyer early. Miss that window and showings thin out, and later offers tend to come in below the one you declined.

Concessions are common now. Rate buydowns, closing costs, repairs. Often all three.

For the agents and lenders here: what is the most effective way you have found to reset a seller's price expectation before listing?
